extracted.intended_audience: students and early-career mathematicians considering which field, problem, or department to pursue
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for choosing a mathematical research field, problems, and institutions, emphasizing how to avoid chasing glamour or fame and how to build a foundation for long-term success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid choosing a field for glamour or fame
rubrics_metrics.description: "Going into a field or department simply because it is glamorous is not a good idea... honestly, there isn’t that much fame or glamour in mathematics overall, and it is not worth chasing these things as your primary goal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anything glamorous is likely to be highly competitive; focusing primarily on glamour or fame is a poor basis for career decisions. Treat glamour/fame as a weak, secondary factor at best; prefer intrinsic interest and fit. The post warns against letting prestige be the main driver of career choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not focus solely on the most famous problems or people because they are famous
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nor is focusing on the most famous problems (or mathematicians) within a field, solely because they are famous – honestly, there isn’t that much fame or glamour in mathematics overall, and it is not worth chasing these things as your primary goal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fame alone is a poor signal of suitability; famous problems are often very hard and require substantial background. Instead evaluate problems/people/institutions for substantive fit (tools, methods, accessible subproblems) rather than notoriety alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: A famous unsolved problem is almost never solved ab nihilo
rubrics_metrics.description: "A famous unsolved problem is almost never solved ab nihilo. One has to first spend much time and effort working on simpler (and much less famous) model problems, acquiring techniques, intuition, partial results, context, and literature... before having any real chance of solving any really big problem in the area."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical career strategy: work on simpler model problems to gain techniques, intuition, partial results, and context; use these to identify fruitful approaches and to rule out fruitless ones. Expect long-term accumulation of background rather than immediate breakthroughs. The post acknowledges occasional exceptions where the right people/tools make a quick solution possible, but treats these as rare. Also watch for existing 'no go' theorems and counterexamples that eliminate whole strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a strong foundation via less glamorous work
rubrics_metrics.description: "Anything glamorous is likely to be highly competitive, and only those with the most solid of backgrounds (in particular, lots of experience with less glamorous aspects of the field) are likely to get anywhere."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan to spend significant time on foundational, technical, or 'unattractive' subareas to develop expertise and credibility. Such work both prepares you for harder problems and increases your chance of making substantive contributions in competitive areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't make prizes or recognition your primary motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: "For similar reasons, one should never make prizes or recognition a primary reason for pursuing mathematics; it is a better strategy in the long-term to just produce good mathematics and contribute to your field, and the prizes and recognition will take care of themselves (and be well-earned when they eventually do appear)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat awards and recognition as by-products of sustained contribution, not as objectives. Monetary amounts of prizes are less important than the prestige/recognition they confer. If primary goal is wealth, consider non-academic careers (finance, IT, industry) which may better fulfill that objective; academic jobs offer other non-monetary benefits (tenure, academic freedom, flexible schedules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate why a problem, person, or institution is famous before choosing it
rubrics_metrics.description: "On the other hand, it can be worth researching why a problem or mathematician is famous, or how an institution or department earnt its prestige; such specific information can help you decide whether this problem, mathematician, or department would be of interest to you."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do targeted research into the sources of prestige: which concrete strengths, topics, people, or historical achievements generated the reputation. Use that information to assess fit (match with your interests, available mentors, appropriate subproblems) rather than relying on general prestige.
